example_01.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to all authenticated users
example_01.justification: The role.yaml grants get, list, create, delete, and watch permissions on pods. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to system:authenticated, meaning any authenticated user can manage pods in the webapp namespace. This is a security weakness because it allows users with no need-to-know access to delete or create pods.

example_02.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to all authenticated users
example_02.justification: The clusterrole.yaml grants get, list, and watch permissions on a wide range of resources. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to system:authenticated, meaning any authenticated user can enumerate all pods, nodes, services, endpoints, namespaces, deployments, replicasets, daemonsets, and metrics in the cluster. This is an overly broad binding that creates a security weakness by allowing unprivileged users access to sensitive information.

example_03.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to unauthenticated users
example_03.justification: The role.yaml grants get, list, create, update, and patch permissions on deployments in the cicd namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to system:unauthenticated, meaning any unauthenticated user — with no credentials at all — can deploy new applications in the cicd namespace. The misconfiguration is only visible by reading both files together: the role file alone does not reveal the dangerous subject, and the binding file alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being granted.

example_04.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to authenticated users
example_04.justification: The role.yaml grants get, list, and watch permissions on all secrets and configmaps in the database namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to system:authenticated, meaning any authenticated user can enumerate all secrets and configmaps in the database namespace. This misconfiguration is only visible by reading both files together — the role file alone does not reveal the dangerous subject, and the binding file alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being granted.

example_05.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to unauthenticated users
example_05.justification: The clusterrole.yaml grants get, list, and watch permissions on nodes, persistentvolumes. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to system:unauthenticated, meaning any unauthenticated user — with no credentials at all — can enumerate all nodes and persistentvolumes across the entire cluster. This misconfiguration is only visible by reading both files together.

example_06.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to all authenticated users
example_06.justification: The role.yaml grants get, list, create, update, patch, and delete permissions on configmaps in the logging namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to system:authenticated, meaning any authenticated user can write to configmaps in the logging namespace. This is a security weakness because it allows any authenticated user to modify configmaps, potentially leading to unintended behavior or security vulnerabilities.

example_07.category: Overly broad cluster role binding to authenticated users
example_07.justification: The clusterrole.yaml grants get, list, create, update, and patch permissions on serviceaccounts and namespaces. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to system:authenticated, meaning any authenticated user can create, update, or patch service accounts in the entire cluster. This misconfiguration is only visible by reading both files together — the role alone does not reveal the dangerous subject, and the binding alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being granted.

example_08.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to unauthenticated users
example_08.justification: The role.yaml grants get, list, and watch permissions on pods. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to system:unauthenticated, meaning any unauthenticated user — with no credentials at all — can enumerate all pods in the development namespace. The misconfiguration is only visible by reading both files together: the role file alone does not reveal the dangerous subject, and the binding file alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being granted.

example_09.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to all authenticated users
example_09.justification: The role.yaml grants get, list, create, update, patch, and delete permissions on ingresses in the ingress-nginx namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to system:authenticated, meaning any authenticated user — with credentials of any kind — can manage all ingresses in the ingress-nginx namespace. The misconfiguration is only visible by reading both files together: the role file alone does not reveal the dangerous subject, and the binding file alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being granted.

example_10.category: Overly broad cluster role binding to all authenticated users
example_10.justification: The clusterrole.yaml defines a ClusterRole with very broad permissions, including create, update, and delete access to many resources. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to the system:authenticated group, meaning any authenticated user can perform these actions across all namespaces in the cluster. This is a security weakness because it allows users who are not explicitly granted these permissions to modify or delete sensitive resources.

example_11.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to a service account with unnecessary permissions
example_11.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a webapp-nginx workload running in the webapp namespace. The role.yaml grants get, list, watch, create, delete permissions on pods and deployments, as well as get, list, create, update permissions on services. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to the webapp-nginx-sa ServiceAccount, which is mounted by the deployment. However, the workload does not require such broad permissions — it only needs to run a simple nginx container with port 80 exposed. Reading all four files together reveals that the service account has been granted unnecessary permissions, creating a security weakness.

example_12.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to service account with excessive permissions
example_12.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a Redis cache workload and mounts the redis-cache-sa ServiceAccount. The role.yaml grants get, list, watch, create, delete permissions on pods, deployments, and configmaps in the caching namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to the redis-cache-sa ServiceAccount, which is used by the deployment. Reading all four files together reveals that the service account has been granted excessive permissions — it can not only read and list pods but also create and delete them, as well as manage deployments and configmaps. This creates a security weakness because an attacker who gains access to this service account could potentially disrupt or compromise other workloads in the caching namespace.

example_13.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to a service account with no legitimate need for delete permissions
example_13.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a prometheus-scraper workload running prom/prometheus:v2.47.0 and does not explicitly state any need for delete permissions on pods, deployments, services, or endpoints. However, the role.yaml grants get, list, watch, and delete permissions on these resources to the prometheus-scraper-role Role. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to the prometheus-scraper-sa ServiceAccount, which is mounted by the deployment. Reading all three files together reveals that the workload has no legitimate need for delete permissions, making this a security weakness.

example_14.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to service account with unnecessary permissions
example_14.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a static file server workload running nginx:1.25 and mounts the fileserver-sa ServiceAccount. The role.yaml grants get, list, create, update, patch, and delete permissions on services, ingresses, and endpoints in the fileserver namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to the fileserver-sa ServiceAccount. Reading all four files together reveals that the service account has been granted unnecessary permissions for a static file server workload — it only needs read access to services and ingresses, but is also granted create, update, patch, and delete permissions on these resources.

example_15.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to a service account with sensitive credentials
example_15.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a PostgreSQL database deployment and mounts the postgres-sa ServiceAccount. The role.yaml grants a wide range of permissions, including delete access to pods and persistentvolumeclaims, which is not necessary for a database workload. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to the postgres-sa ServiceAccount, which has sensitive credentials (POSTGRES_PASSWORD) stored in its environment variables. This creates a security weakness because an attacker with access to the service account's secrets could delete the database pods or persistentvolumeclaims, leading to data loss.

example_16.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to a service account with no apparent need for such permissions
example_16.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a frontend-react workload running a Node.js application. The role.yaml grants get, list, create, update, patch, and delete permissions on services, endpoints, and deployments in the frontend namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to the frontend-react-sa ServiceAccount. However, upon closer inspection of the deployment.yaml, there is no indication that the workload requires such broad permissions — it only exposes port 3000 for a Node.js application, which does not typically require access to services, endpoints, or deployments. The misconfiguration becomes apparent when reading all three files together: the role grants excessive permissions, and the binding applies these permissions to a ServiceAccount with no clear need for them.

example_17.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to service account with excessive permissions
example_17.justification: The role.yaml grants the nginx-proxy-role Role, which has excessive permissions on pods, deployments, and services. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to the nginx-proxy-sa ServiceAccount, which is used by the deployment. Reading all four files together reveals that the service account has been granted create, update, and patch permissions on deployments, which is unnecessary for a reverse proxy workload. This creates a security weakness because an attacker could potentially exploit these excessive permissions to modify or delete deployments in the proxy namespace.

example_18.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to a service account with unnecessary permissions
example_18.justification: The deployment.yaml defines an Elasticsearch workload and mounts the elasticsearch-sa ServiceAccount. The role.yaml grants get, list, create, update, patch, and delete permissions on persistentvolumeclaims, deployments, statefulsets, and pods in the logging namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to the elasticsearch-sa ServiceAccount. Reading all four files together reveals that the service account has been granted unnecessary permissions for a workload that only needs to access Elasticsearch resources.

example_19.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to a service account with unnecessary permissions
example_19.justification: The role.yaml grants get, list, watch, create, delete permissions on pods and services in the messaging namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to the rabbitmq-sa ServiceAccount. However, the deployment.yaml defines a RabbitMQ workload that does not require such broad permissions — it only needs access to its own pod and service resources for management purposes. Reading all three files together reveals an unnecessary risk: the service account has been granted more permissions than necessary, which could lead to security issues if exploited.

example_20.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to a service account with unnecessary permissions
example_20.justification: The role.yaml grants get, list, watch, update, patch, and delete permissions on deployments, pods, and services. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to the nginx-exporter-sa ServiceAccount in the exports namespace. However, the deployment.yaml defines an nginx-exporter workload that only needs to scrape metrics from a stub status endpoint (http://localhost/stub_status) and does not require any of these permissions. Reading all three files together reveals that the role and binding create unnecessary risk by granting excessive permissions to the service account used by this workload.

example_21.category: Unnecessary service account token for frontend deployment
example_21.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a frontend workload with automountServiceAccountToken set to false, which means the pod will not have access to its associated service account token. However, the networkpolicy.yaml selects pods with label app: web-frontend for ingress traffic, but these labels do not match the labels on the frontend deployment (app: frontend). This discrepancy suggests that the network policy is intended for a different workload or deployment, and the frontend deployment does not need to be bound to any service account. The misconfiguration only becomes visible by reading both files together — the deployment establishes the pod has no legitimate need for a service account token, while the network policy establishes it is being selected for ingress traffic despite having incorrect labels.

example_22.category: Unnecessary network policy allowing unsecured communication with backend API
example_22.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a PostgreSQL database workload and explicitly sets automountServiceAccountToken to false. This suggests the workload does not need access to any secrets or service accounts, but it is still exposed to network traffic. The networkpolicy.yaml allows ingress and egress communication with pods labeled as app: backend-api, which could potentially allow unsecured communication between the PostgreSQL database and the backend API. Reading both files together reveals a potential security weakness — the deployment does not need access to secrets or service accounts, but it is still exposed to network traffic, and the network policy allows unsecured communication with the backend API.

example_23.category: Unnecessary network policy allowing unauthenticated access to Prometheus
example_23.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a Prometheus workload with automountServiceAccountToken set to false, which means it does not have a service account token. However, the networkpolicy.yaml allows ingress from pods labeled as role: metrics-consumer, which could potentially be unauthenticated or unauthorized. This creates a security weakness because an attacker could exploit this policy to access the Prometheus workload without proper authentication.

example_24.category: Unnecessary network policy allowing unauthenticated ingress from API gateway
example_24.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a payment-api workload with automountServiceAccountToken set to false, which means it does not have a service account token. However, the networkpolicy.yaml allows ingress traffic from pods labeled as role: api-gateway, which could be unauthenticated. This creates a potential security weakness because an attacker could exploit this policy to gain unauthorized access to the payment-api workload.

example_25.category: Unnecessary network policy allowing unauthenticated access to Elasticsearch
example_25.justification: The deployment.yaml defines an Elasticsearch workload with automountServiceAccountToken set to false, which means it does not have a service account token. However, the networkpolicy.yaml allows ingress from pods labeled as role: log-shipper, which could potentially be unauthenticated or malicious. This creates a security weakness because an attacker could exploit this policy to access the Elasticsearch pod without proper authentication.

example_26.category: Unnecessary network policy allowing unsecured communication with worker pods
example_26.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a rabbitmq workload that does not require access to any secrets. However, the networkpolicy.yaml allows ingress and egress traffic from/to pods labeled as app: worker, which could potentially allow unsecured communication with these pods. This misconfiguration is only visible by reading both files together — the deployment establishes the workload has no legitimate need for secret access, while the network policy establishes it has been granted unnecessary access to communicate with other pods.

example_27.category: Unnecessary service account token for Jenkins deployment
example_27.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a Jenkins workload with automountServiceAccountToken set to false, which means the pod will not have access to the service account token. However, the networkpolicy.yaml selects pods with label role: build-agent and allows ingress traffic from them. This creates a security weakness because an attacker could potentially exploit this policy to gain unauthorized access to the Jenkins deployment by creating a pod with the matching label and accessing the Jenkins UI.

example_28.category: Unnecessary network policy allowing unauthenticated ingress traffic
example_28.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a react-app workload running in the frontend namespace. The networkpolicy.yaml defines an ingress policy for pods with label app: reactapp, which is not present on any pod in this cluster (the deployment has app: react-app). However, the policy allows unauthenticated ingress traffic, which could be exploited by malicious actors. This misconfiguration only becomes visible when reading both files together — the deployment alone does not reveal the network policy's existence or its potential security implications.

example_29.category: Unnecessary network policy allowing unauthenticated access from load balancers
example_29.justification: The deployment.yaml defines an api-gateway workload with automountServiceAccountToken set to false, which means it does not have a service account token. However, the networkpolicy.yaml allows ingress traffic from pods labeled as role: load-balancer, which could be unauthenticated. This creates a potential security weakness because an attacker could use this policy to access the api-gateway without being properly authenticated.

example_30.category: Unnecessary network policy allowing unauthenticated ingress from job scheduler
example_30.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a worker Deployment with automountServiceAccountToken set to false, which means the pods will not have a service account token. However, the networkpolicy.yaml allows ingress traffic from the job-scheduler pod, which is unauthenticated and could potentially exploit this vulnerability.

example_31.category: Overly broad ClusterRole with excessive permissions
example_31.justification: The clusterrole.yaml defines a ClusterRole named cicd-pipeline-manager that grants get, list, create, update, and patch permissions on deployments in the apps group. However, the target_clusterrole.yaml defines an even more permissive ClusterRole named cluster-superuser that grants all possible verbs on all resources and nonResourceURLs. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds the cicd-pipeline-manager ClusterRole to a ServiceAccount in the cicd namespace, but this binding is overshadowed by the excessive permissions granted by the cluster-superuser ClusterRole. Reading both files together reveals that the cicd-pipeline-manager ClusterRole's permissions are unnecessary and potentially insecure due to the existence of the more permissive cluster-superuser ClusterRole.

example_32.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to service account with elevated permissions
example_32.justification: The role.yaml grants escalate permission on roles, which is an unusual and potentially dangerous verb. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to the prometheus-sa ServiceAccount in the monitoring namespace. However, the target_role.yaml defines a Role with extremely broad permissions (get, list, watch, create, update, delete) on all resources across all namespaces. This creates a security weakness because the service account bound to the monitoring-role-manager Role has elevated permissions due to the binding to the monitoring-namespace-admin Role, which is not necessary for its intended function of managing Prometheus configurations.

example_33.category: Overly broad impersonation permissions for service account
example_33.justification: The clusterrole.yaml grants impersonate, get, and list permissions on users, serviceaccounts, and userextras. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to the api-gateway-sa ServiceAccount in the webapp namespace. This means the api-gateway-sa can impersonate any user or serviceaccount, which is a security weakness because it allows the service account to access resources without proper authentication.

example_34.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to a user account
example_34.justification: The role.yaml grants get, list, and bind permissions on roles in the devops namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to the devops-automation-user User, meaning any user with that name can enumerate all roles in the devops namespace and even bind new roles. This is a security weakness because it allows an attacker to potentially escalate their privileges by binding themselves to more powerful roles.

example_35.category: Overly broad cluster-wide read access for security team group
example_35.justification: The target_clusterrole.yaml grants get, list, and watch permissions on all resources across the entire cluster. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to the security-team Group. Reading both files together reveals that any member of the security team can enumerate all clusters, namespaces, services, pods, secrets, etc., which is an overly broad access level for a group intended to perform security audits.

example_36.category: Overly broad impersonation of service accounts by workflow engine
example_36.justification: The clusterrole.yaml grants the ClusterRole 'workflow-sa-impersonator' to impersonate and get/list all serviceaccounts, as well as create tokens for them. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to the workflow-engine-sa ServiceAccount in the platform namespace. This means that the workflow engine can impersonate any service account in the cluster, which is a security risk because it allows the workflow engine to access sensitive information and perform actions on behalf of other services without their knowledge or consent.

example_37.category: Overly broad cluster role with excessive permissions
example_37.justification: The clusterrole.yaml defines a ClusterRole named platform-rbac-manager that grants get, list, bind, and escalate permissions on roles, clusterroles, rolebindings, and clusterrolebindings. The target_clusterrole.yaml defines another ClusterRole named platform-admin with even broader permissions, including create, update, patch, and delete on all resources and nonResourceURLs. However, the clusterrolebinding.yaml binds the platform-rbac-manager ClusterRole to a ServiceAccount in the platform namespace, which could potentially be used to escalate privileges to the platform-admin ClusterRole. This creates a security weakness because an attacker with access to the platform-automation-sa ServiceAccount could gain excessive permissions on all resources and URLs within the cluster.

example_38.category: Overly broad impersonation permissions for a specific user
example_38.justification: The clusterrole.yaml grants impersonate and get/list permissions on users. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to the infra-automation-user User, meaning this user can impersonate any user in the cluster. This is a security weakness because it allows the user to assume the identity of other users, potentially leading to unauthorized access or actions.

example_39.category: Overly broad cluster role binding to platform engineers
example_39.justification: The role.yaml defines a ClusterRole with get, list, and watch permissions on serviceaccounts. The rolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to the platform-engineers group via a ClusterRoleBinding. This means any member of the platform-engineers group can enumerate all service accounts in the cluster. While it is legitimate for platform engineers to have access to certain resources, granting them get, list, and watch permissions on all serviceaccounts creates an unnecessary risk.

example_40.category: Overly broad cluster role with escalate and impersonate permissions
example_40.justification: The clusterrole.yaml defines a ClusterRole named tenant-admin-manager that grants escalate, impersonate, get, list, create, update, patch, and delete permissions on various resources. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to the tenant-provisioner-sa ServiceAccount in the tenants namespace. This creates a security weakness because the tenant-admin-manager ClusterRole has overly broad permissions, including escalate and impersonate, which could be used for privilege escalation or lateral movement within the cluster.

example_41.category: Unnecessary secret access for static web server
example_41.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a webapp-nginx workload running nginx:1.25 and does not explicitly require access to any secrets. However, the role.yaml grants get, list, and watch permissions on all secrets in the webapp namespace, and the rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the webapp-nginx-sa ServiceAccount, which is the same ServiceAccount mounted by the deployment. The misconfiguration only becomes visible by reading all four files together — the deployment establishes the workload has no legitimate need for secret access, while the role and binding establish it has been granted exactly that.

example_81.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to a service account with no apparent need for configmap and service creation/deletion permissions

The rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the grafana-sa ServiceAccount, which is mounted by the deployment. The misconfiguration only becomes visible by reading all four files together — the role file alone does not reveal the dangerous subject, and the binding file alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being granted.

example_83.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to a service account with pod exec permissions

However, the role also grants pods/exec permissions, allowing the service account to execute code within any pod. This creates a security weakness because it allows the service account to potentially access and manipulate other pods in the caching namespace.

example_84.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to a service account with unnecessary permissions
example_84.justification: The role.yaml grants get, list, create, update, patch, and delete permissions on persistentvolumeclaims, deployments, and pods. example_85.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to a service account with unnecessary permissions
example_85.justification: The deployment.yaml defines the jaeger workload and mounts the jaeger-sa ServiceAccount. However, reading all four files together reveals that the jaeger workload does not need such broad permissions: it only needs to expose its service (16686) and port (14268). The misconfiguration is only visible by considering the relationships between these resources.

example_86.category: Unnecessary service account token for a container that doesn't need it
example_86.justification: The deployment.yaml defines the solr Deployment in the search namespace. The automountServiceAccountToken field is set to false, which means the pod will not automatically mount a service account token. However, this setting contradicts the fact that the container uses a service account (implicitly, since it's not explicitly specified). In Kubernetes 1.25 and later, when automountServiceAccountToken is set to false, the pod will still be able to use the service account for authentication purposes. This creates a security weakness because an attacker could potentially exploit this misconfiguration by using the service account credentials.

example_87.category: Unnecessary service account token automount for Kafka deployment
example_87.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a Kafka deployment with automountServiceAccountToken set to false. The misconfiguration only becomes visible by reading both files together — the deployment establishes that it does not need a service account token, while the network policy establishes that it allows incoming traffic on port 9092.

example_88.category: Unnecessary network policy allowing unauthenticated access to Falco deployment

example_89.category: Unnecessary network policy allowing unauthenticated access to envoy service

example_90.category: Unnecessary network policy allowing unauthenticated access to Jupyter service
